title: Building Your Story Bank
summary: Improvising a story live under a follow-up barrage is the top cause of rambling. Learn how to mine 8-12 real stories from your work history, tag them by competency, and reuse one incident across several angles without sounding rehearsed.

slides.markdown:
A story bank is a pre-built, indexed set of 8-12 real work incidents you can retrieve on demand, each tagged by the competency it demonstrates. It exists because the alternative — improvising a story live, mid-interview — is the single biggest cause of rambling, vague outcomes, and answers that collapse under a follow-up.

The bank is not a script. You never memorize a story word for word; you memorize its *facts* — who, what changed, what you specifically did, what the measurable result was — and let the phrasing adapt to whatever angle the question needs.

Built right, a bank of 8-12 stories can answer almost anything a loop throws at you, because most questions are really asking about a small set of underlying competencies wearing different wording. Building it once pays off across every loop you'll ever run.

slides.sectionTitle: Why improvising is the top cause of rambling
slides.markdown:
Under interview pressure, an improvised story tends to expand rather than compress: you start talking before you know the ending, add detail that doesn't matter, and lose track of what the actual point was supposed to be. The interviewer has to work to extract the signal, which is exactly backwards from what you want.

A pre-built story has already had its fat trimmed. You know before you open your mouth: the one-sentence setup, the two or three actions that mattered, and the number that proves the outcome. That structure is what keeps an answer to 90 seconds instead of four minutes, and it's what survives a "can you be more specific" follow-up instead of dissolving into more vague narration.

The fix isn't to talk less — it's to have already decided, before the interview, what the story is actually *about*.

slides.sectionTitle: Mining your work history for 8-12 candidates
slides.markdown:
Most people underestimate how much usable material they already have. A systematic way to mine it: go through your last 2-3 years, project by project, and for each one ask three questions — where did I disagree with someone, where did something go wrong, and where did I make a call nobody told me to make.

Good sources beyond "big wins": incidents/outages you helped resolve, a project that got cancelled or descoped, a teammate you had friction with, a decision you made with incomplete information, a time you had to say no to a stakeholder, mentoring or onboarding someone, a piece of tech debt you pushed to fix against inertia.

Aim for 8-12 distinct incidents. Fewer than 8 and you'll run out of material across a multi-round loop; more than 12 and you'll never rehearse any of them deeply enough to survive follow-ups.

Once you have 8-12 candidates, tag each one by which competencies it can answer — ownership, conflict, ambiguity, failure/growth, leadership/influence, collaboration. Most real stories legitimately support two or three tags, not just one.

Build this as a simple table you can scan the morning of an interview:

| Story | Primary tag | Secondary tag |
|---|---|---|
| Migrated legacy billing service | Ownership | Ambiguity |
| Pushback from PM on scope cut | Conflict | Influence |
| Missed launch date, root-caused it | Failure/Growth | Ownership |

With this table in front of you, "tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision" instantly maps to a specific row instead of triggering a live search through your memory. That mapping is the entire point of the bank.

slides.subTitle: Reusing it for conflict, failure, and leadership
slides.markdown:
A rich real incident almost always supports several angles, because real work is rarely clean. Take one incident: a launch slipped two weeks because you and a peer disagreed about whether to ship with a known edge-case bug.

- **As a conflict story:** focus on the disagreement itself — what each side argued, how you resolved it, what you'd do differently in the conversation.
- **As a failure story:** focus on the slip itself — what you missed in planning that let the edge case surface so late, and the process change you made after.
- **As a leadership/influence story:** focus on how you got alignment without formal authority over the peer's team.

Same facts, three different emphases. This is why 8-12 well-chosen stories can cover a whole loop — you're not inventing new material per question, you're re-cutting the same footage.

slides.sectionTitle: Turning one incident into three STAR answers
slides.subTitle: Concrete example
slides.markdown:
Continuing the launch-slip example, here's how the same Situation/Task changes Action/Result emphasis by angle:

```
Base facts (fixed across all three):
Situation: Two weeks before launch, found an edge case affecting ~3% of users.
Task: Decide whether to ship on time with a known gap or delay.

CONFLICT angle:
Action: Pushed back on PM's "ship on time" call; proposed a feature-flagged partial rollout.
Result: PM agreed after seeing the 3% number; shipped on time, gap fixed in week 1 post-launch.

FAILURE angle:
Action: Root-caused why QA missed it — test plan didn't cover that user segment.
Result: Added the segment to the test matrix; caught two similar gaps in the next release.

LEADERSHIP angle:
Action: Got two other engineers to help validate the flag rollout overnight without being asked.
Result: Team adopted feature-flagged rollouts as default for risky launches going forward.
```

Notice the Situation and Task never change — only which Action/Result pair you lead with.

slides.sectionTitle: A vague story vs. a metric-anchored story
slides.subTitle: Same incident, two write-ups
slides.markdown:
The gap between a mediocre story and a strong one is almost always specificity, not the underlying incident:

| | Vague version | Metric-anchored version |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | "We had a performance issue on the checkout flow" | "Checkout p95 latency hit 4.2s during a traffic spike, above our 1s SLO" |
| Action | "I looked into it and fixed the query" | "I profiled it, found an unindexed join scanning 2M rows, added a composite index" |
| Result | "It got a lot better" | "p95 dropped to 180ms; checkout abandonment fell 6% that week" |

The underlying incident can be identical. What separates the two write-ups is whether you did the work, ahead of time, to remember or reconstruct the actual numbers. That's a prep task, not a talent — go back to dashboards, tickets, or performance reviews to recover real figures before the interview.

slides.sectionTitle: A story bank where you're only ever the hero
slides.markdown:
A bank made entirely of unblemished wins is a red flag interviewers are trained to notice — see red flags & common mistakes, later in this group, for the full pattern. If every story ends with you being right, the team being wrong, and a clean triumphant result, interviewers start doubting the stories rather than admiring them.

A balanced bank needs at least one or two stories where you were genuinely wrong, missed something, or had to change your mind — not humble-bragging ("I worked too hard") but a real miss with a real lesson. "A time you failed" and "a time you disagreed with a decision and lost" are both nearly guaranteed questions across enough interviews; if you don't have real material for them, you'll improvise, and improvising on your weakest-feeling topic is the worst place to do it.

Build the failure stories into the bank on day one, not as an afterthought the night before.

slides.sectionTitle: How many stories is enough, and how deep
slides.markdown:
8-12 is a practical target, not a hard rule, balanced against real prep time. Fewer than 6 and you risk repeating the same story so often across a multi-round loop that it starts sounding rehearsed even when the facts are true. More than 15 and the marginal story gets shallow prep, which defeats the purpose — a thin story in the bank is worse than not having it, because you'll reach for it under pressure and then can't sustain follow-ups.

Depth matters more than count: for each story you keep, you should be able to answer at least three unscripted follow-ups ("what would you do differently," "how did the other person react," "what was the actual number") without pausing to invent an answer. If you can't, the story isn't ready — trim your bank rather than pad it.

A story bank ages. Interviewers, especially at senior levels, respond better to recent material — a story from three years ago reads as "is this all you've got lately" even if it's strong. Refresh the bank every 6-12 months, or after any project that clearly produced new material: a launch, an incident, a hard conversation, a promotion case.

A lightweight habit that keeps this cheap: right after any notable incident at work, write two sentences — what happened, what you did, what the number was — into a running notes doc while it's fresh. Reconstructing details six months later from memory is far harder than jotting them down the week they happened, and the jotted version is what eventually becomes your next bank entry.

With a tagged bank in hand, the live skill in the interview is fast retrieval, not composition: hear the question, identify the competency it's really asking about, pull the matching row, deliver the STAR shape you already know cold.

The next topic in this group, common question archetypes, catalogs the recurring question families and what each is really probing — pairing that with your tagged bank is what makes retrieval close to instant instead of a live scramble.
